extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and researchers in enumerative combinatorics (reading about one-variable rational generating functions)
extracted.subtask_description: Identification and manipulation of rational generating functions in one variable: equivalent characterizations, consequences (polynomial/quasipolynomial cases), coefficient recurrences, duality, and closure properties, with worked examples (Fibonacci, lattice paths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent characterizations of rational generating functions (Theorem 4.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : N -> C and fixed d, the following are equivalent: (i) the generating function F(x)=sum_{n>=0} f(n)x^n equals P(x)/Q(x) with Q(x)=1+α1 x+...+αd x^d and P,Q polynomials with deg P < d; (ii) f satisfies a homogeneous linear recurrence with constant coefficients of order d: for all n>=0, f(n+d)+α1 f(n+d-1)+...+αd f(n)=0; (iii) f(n) can be written for all n>=0 as a finite sum f(n)=sum_{i=1}^k Pi(n) γ_i^n where the γ_i are the (distinct, nonzero) reciprocals of the roots of Q and each Pi(n) is a polynomial of degree < di (multiplicity-related).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use any of the three forms interchangeably to recognize or produce rational generating functions: show rationality by giving P/Q, derive the linear constant-coefficient recurrence, or give an explicit closed form as a sum of polynomial times exponential terms. Example: Fibonacci numbers satisfy Fn+2 = Fn+1 + Fn, so F(x)=x/(1-x-x^2) and Fn = αϕ^n+βϕ^n (Binet formula). When implementing, identify Q(x) to get recurrence (ii), factor Q to find the γ_i for (iii), and account for multiplicities (leading to polynomial factors Pi(n)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal (reduced) rational form <-> minimal recurrence <-> polynomial degree (Corollary 4.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following are equivalent: (i) P(x) and Q(x) are relatively prime (so P/Q is written in lowest terms); (ii) there is no smaller-order linear recurrence with constant coefficients satisfied by f (i.e., (4.2) is the homogeneous linear recurrence with constant coefficients of least degree); (iii) in the decomposition f(n)=sum_i Pi(n) γ_i^n, deg Pi(n)=di-1 where di are the multiplicities of the γ_i in Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check minimality, reduce P/Q and inspect Q's degree: deg Q is the minimal order of the recurrence. Conversely, given a recurrence, remove common polynomial factors between numerator and denominator to obtain the reduced rational form. The degrees of the polynomial multipliers Pi match multiplicities in the denominator factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional set and degree-excess m(f) for P/Q with deg P >= deg Q (Proposition 4.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given P(x)/Q(x)=sum_{n>=0} f(n)x^n with P,Q 1 C[x] and possibly deg P >= deg Q, there exists a unique finite exceptional set E_f (a finite set of nonnegative integers) and a unique polynomial-sequence f1 supported on E_f such that f equals g on indices not in E_f and g has generating function R(x)/Q(x) with deg R < deg Q. Define m(f)=max E_f (or deg P if deg P >= deg Q). Then (i) m(f)=deg P when deg P >= deg Q; (ii) m(f) is the largest n for which the recurrence (4.2) fails; (iii) m(f) is the largest n for which the asymptotic decomposition f(n)=sum_i Pi(n) γ_i^n fails (i.e., the decomposition holds for n sufficiently large).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deg P >= deg Q, perform polynomial division P/Q = L + R/Q to separate the polynomial part L(x) (which encodes finitely many exceptional coefficients) and a proper rational part R/Q with deg R < deg Q; the exceptional set corresponds to coefficients coming from L(x). m(f) measures how far 'initial anomalies' extend before the recurrence/closed form applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coefficient recurrence obtained directly from P(x)/Q(x) (Equation (4.8))
rubrics_metrics.description: If P(x)=sum_{0<=j<=e} β_j x^j and Q(x)=1+α1 x+...+αd x^d, equating coefficients in P/Q = sum_{n>=0} f(n)x^n yields for n>=0: f(n) = α1 f(n-1) + ... + αd f(n-d) + β_n (with f(k)=0 for k<0 and β_k = 0 for k>e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a direct, implementable linear recurrence to compute coefficients f(n) by inspection for moderate d and known α_i,β_j. Use initial β_j for the inhomogeneous terms up to degree e; beyond that the recurrence is homogeneous. Example in text: compute f(n) from P(x)=1+x+x^2 and Q(x)=1-3x+3x^3 to see pattern and exceptional set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duality under x -> 1/x for rational generating functions (Proposition 4.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f: Z -> C satisfies the linear recurrence f(n+d)+α1 f(n+d-1)+...+αd f(n)=0 for all n in Z and F(x)=sum_{n>=0} f(n)x^n = P(x)/Q(x), then as rational functions one has P(x)/Q(x) = -x^d P(1/x)/Q(1/x), equivalently F(1/x) is also a rational function (considered as a rational function/Laurent series equality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statement about rational-function equality (not power-series radius of convergence). It can be used to deduce symmetry properties of coefficients and to relate behavior at infinity to behavior at zero. Be careful: one works in the field of rational functions or Laurent series, not in the ring of formal power series around 0 alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences when deg P < deg Q (Corollary 4.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume F(x)=P(x)/Q(x) with deg P < deg Q and Q(x)=1+α1 x+...+αd x^d. Let β_j be coefficients of P. Then: (i) the smallest index r with β_r != 0 equals min{n>=0 : f(n) != 0} and f(r)=β_r; (ii) the smallest s such that f(-s) != 0 equals min{ j : β_j != 0 } relative to degree of Q and gives relation deg Q - deg P; (iii) F(1/x) relates to F(x) by shifts and scaling: F(1/x) = ± x^{-s} times a scalar times F(x) iff f(n) equals a shifted copy of itself on Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deg P < deg Q the polynomial numerator directly controls low-index coefficients; zeros of initial coefficients correspond to low-degree terms absent in P. Use these facts to read off earliest nonzero coefficient and to detect palindromic/reciprocal-type rational functions (via F(1/x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of rational power series under Hadamard product (Proposition 4.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F(x)=sum f(n)x^n and G(x)=sum g(n)x^n are rational power series, then their Hadamard product H(x)=sum f(n)g(n)x^n is also rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: express f(n), g(n) for large n as finite sums of polynomial times exponentials (per Theorem 4.1.1), multiply termwise to get the same form for h(n) for large n, hence H(x) rational. Use this when combining coefficientwise sequences coming from rational sources (e.g., diagonal extractions, termwise multipliers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial sequences <-> generating functions of form P(x)/(1-x)^{d+1} (Corollary 4.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : N -> C the following are equivalent: (i) the generating function equals P(x)/(1-x)^{d+1} with P(x) in C[x], deg P <= d; (ii) the (d+1)-th forward difference ∆^{d+1} f(n) = 0 for all n>=0; (iii) f(n) is a polynomial in n of degree at most d (with exact degree d iff P(1) != 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use any of these equivalent criteria to detect polynomial sequences: check finite differences, produce the rational form with denominator (1-x)^{d+1}, or verify polynomial formula. The leading coefficient relates to P(1)/d!. This characterization gives an algorithmic way to convert polynomial enumerators to rational generating functions and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard polynomial bases and transitions (Section 4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vector space of polynomial sequences of degree <= d admits several common bases: (a) monomials n^i (0<=i<=d); (b) binomial-coefficient polynomials (n choose i); (c) falling factorials (n)_i = n(n-1)...(n-i+1); (d) rising factorials n(n+1)...(n+i-1). Transition matrices between these bases are given by (signed) Stirling numbers of the first and second kinds and by discrete analogues of the Taylor expansion (finite differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the basis suited to the problem: (n choose i) basis is natural when generating functions have denominator (1-x)^{d+1}; falling/rising factorials are natural for difference operators; transition formulas allow switching (e.g., use Stirling numbers to go between n^i and (n)_i). The diagonal of the difference table gives coefficients in the falling-factorial expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasipolynomial characterization (Proposition 4.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : N -> C and integer N>0 the following are equivalent: (i) f is a quasipolynomial of quasiperiod N (i.e., on residue classes mod N it equals polynomials); (ii) the generating function F(x)=P(x)/Q(x) with P,Q in C[x], deg P < deg Q, and every zero α of Q satisfies α^N = 1 (i.e., roots of Q are roots of unity); (iii) for all n>=0, f(n)=sum_{i=1}^k Pi(n) γ_i^n where each Pi is a polynomial and each γ_i satisfies γ_i^N = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To detect quasipolynomiality, factor the denominator Q: if all poles are roots of unity, the coefficient sequence is eventually quasipolynomial with period dividing the lcm of pole orders. Conversely, given a quasipolynomial with period N, its generating function reduces to a rational function whose denominator has roots among N-th roots of unity.
